newsitem.title: USA: Clinton nominates Clark to command NATO forces.
newsitem.headline: Clinton nominates Clark to command NATO forces.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday nominated U.S. Army Gen. Wesley Clark to become commander of all allied NATO forces and American troops in Europe.

Clark, 52, speaks Russian and helped broker the 1995 Dayton, Ohio, peace accords on Bosnia. He now heads U.S. forces in Latin America and will, if approved by the Senate and NATO allies, succeed retiring U.S. Army Gen. George Joulwan as Supreme Allied Commander of NATO in Europe (SACEUR).
"He (Clark) has demonstrated both the military expertise and political acumen needed to fill one of our most important securty postings," Clinton said in a statement issued by the White House.

He said he had "utmost trust" in Clark's ability to tighten ties with allies at a time of tension and change and to forge a NATO partnership with Russia despite Moscow's opposition to alliance enlargement into Eastern Europe.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Washington was consulting with allies on Clark, who would also wear a second military hat as commander of 100,000 U.S. troops in Europe.

"The job of SACEUR and of commander of U.S. troops in Europe requires somebody to be both a soldier and a statesman, to deal not only with military officials but the leaders of governments and Russia," one top Pentagon official said.

"Clark fills the bill," said the official, who asked not to be identified, adding that Defence Secretary William Cohen had recommended him to Clinton after interviewing more than a dozen potential candidates.

The job of SACEUR has been held by U.S. military officers since the end of the Second World War and Clark, a West Point military academy graduate and former Rhodes scholar who attended Britain's Oxford University, is expected to be approved by the allies, according to the Pentagon official.

Joulwan will retire this summer and Clinton's choice of Clark to succeed him leaves the president with another key military decision, a replacement for Army Gen. John Shalikashvili as chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff when Shalikashvili retires in October.

A fast-rising star in the U.S. military, Clark was the senior military member on the American team led by diplomat Richard Holbrooke that brokered the Dayton peace accords. The agreement stopped the fighting in Bosnia and set terms for the NATO-led peacekeeping force of some 31,000, including some 8,000 U.S. troops, which is now there.

"He clearly knows the Bosnia situation and will be well placed to emphasise the importance of getting the country back on a firm economic and political track by mid-1998 before the troops are scheduled to pull out," the Pentagon official said.

Clark, who will also oversee U.S. military operations in Europe and much of Africa, previously headed the Army's National Training Centre at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, and has been director of strategy on the U.S. military Joint Staff.

NATO is currently embroiled in a rift between the United States and France over the command of allied forces in Southern Europe based in Naples. Washington has refused to bow to demands by Paris that the United States turn over the post, which has always been held by a U.S. officer, to a European.

The two countries have been involved in intense negotiations over the job, which the United States says should be held by an American because the preponderance of allied forces in the southern region, including the U.S. Sixth Fleet, are American.
